newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak bank IRB posts '96 loss. [CORRECTED 00:35 GMT 20/03]
newsitem.headline: Slovak bank IRB posts '96 loss. [CORRECTED 00:35 GMT 20/03]

text.p: Investicna a Rozvojova Banka a.s. (IRB), Slovakia's third largest bank, on Wednesday said it posted a 1996 loss of 1.2-1.3 billion crowns, after an after-tax profit of 167.5 million in 1995,

"Considering IRB's basic goal --to complete creation of reserves and provisions to cover potential risks-- shareholders sacrificed their profits, and the bank swung into a controlled loss," IRB President Vojtech Vranay told a news conference.
He added that all 1996 figures were preliminary.

"The bank's 1996 results lay the groundwork for its fast and successfull restructuring...(thus) we review them positively," Vranay said, adding that the loss would be covered by reserve and capital funds.

IRB added that its capital adequacy ratio fell to 2.93 percent at the end of 1996 from 7.25 percent at the end of the previous year. After covering the loss, IRB's reserves and provisions currently total 5.4 billion crowns, compared to 4.58 billion in 1995.
The total volume of loans extended by IRB hit 36.5 billion crowns, of which 23 percent are classified, Vranay said.
IRB's assets totalled 52 billion crowns, after totalling 48.2 billion in 1995. Its net revenue, excluding operating costs, totalled 728 million.

Vranay added the drop in IRB's capital adequacy ratio was "in accordance" with the bank's restructuring project, which secures creating reserves and provisions through "controlled losses". He said the restructuring project did not involve any state funding.
The project aims for IRB's capital adequacy ratio to rise to 6.5 percent in 1997, and to 8.07 by the end of 1998 when the restructuring should be completed.

Vranay said that the second basic goal of the bank was to boost its capital. Its basic capital currently is one billion crowns. (Corrects to clarify that capital boost is not a basic capital increase.)

Frantisek Orolin, IRB vice-president for treasury, told Reuters IRB was currently undercapitalised, and it intends to increase its capital by 1-1.5 billion crowns through both a domestic subordinated debt issue and a share capital increase.
The two issues will be presented to the annual general shareholders meeting planned for May, he said.
